In this paper, we propose a new mathematical model to investigate the transmission
dynamics of dengue. The model is based on an age-structured system of diﬀerential
and  integral  equations  that  couples  the  host  and  mosquito  populations  and  that
incorporates both symptomatic and asymptomatic infections. We derive the basic
reproduction  number  and  conduct  a  rigorous  analysis  on  the  local  and  global
stabilities  of  the  disease-free  steady  state.  Meanwhile,  we  study  the  existence  of
the endemic steady states and explore conditions that could lead to the occurrence
of a backward bifurcation. In addition, we establish the weak and strong uniform

mosquitoes which go on to bite other people and spread the infection to larger human populations. They also
pose  a  threat  to  transfusion  recipients  through  infected  blood  products  [18].  Furthermore,  asymptomatic
individuals can be re-infected, referred to as a secondary infection, through mosquitoes carrying a diﬀerent
strain of dengue virus and become symptomatic with more severe health conditions [24]. The mechanism for
the diﬀerent viral serotypes to cause severe dengue disease is not entirely clear at present, but it is mostly
linked  to  the  Antibody-Dependent  Enhancement  (ADE),  a  phenomenon  where  pre-existing  antibodies  do
not neutralize but rather enhance the new infection [2]. Hence, asymptomatic infectious individuals play a
signiﬁcant role in shaping the overall pattern of dengue transmission and spread. Quantifying such a role is
essential in understanding the transmission dynamics of dengue and in designing eﬀective prevention and
Like  many  other  infectious  disease,  the  transmission  of  dengue  exhibits  strong  heterogeneity  among
diﬀerent human hosts. One of the most important factors to reﬂect such heterogeneity is the chronological
age. Individuals of diﬀerent ages may have diﬀerent social behaviors, mobility levels, and contact dynamics,
which subsequently lead to diﬀerent infection risk, disease severity, survival capacity, and recovery ability.
In  particular,  children  are  more  vulnerable  than  adults  because  of  their  immature  immune  systems,  and
they have higher risk of severe complications for dengue [28,33]. Identifying such transmission characteristics
associated  with  diﬀerent  age  groups  and  classifying  such  an  age  structure  in  a  dengue  model  are  critical
toward a holistic understanding of dengue transmission dynamics.
Numerous  mathematical  models  have  been  published  for  the  transmission  dynamics  of  dengue  [1,11–
13,16,18–20,22,24,26,29,31]. For example, Esteva and Vargas studied the coexistence of diﬀerent serotypes
of  dengue  virus  [11].  Pongsumpun  and  Samana  published  a  model  for  the  primary  infection  dynamics  of
dengue that involves both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals [26]. Jan and Xiao modeled the eﬀect
of partial immunity from the susceptible human population on the transmission of dengue and performed an
optimal control study for disease prevention and intervention [19]. Rashkov and Kooi integrated the vector
dynamics  of  mosquitoes  into  the  human  transmission  of  dengue  [29].  Rocha  et  al.  considered  the  role  of
seasonality in dengue infection dynamics [30]. Ferguson et al. proposed a multi-strain model to investigate
the  eﬀect  of  ADE  on  dengue  transmission  [13].  Aguiar  et  al.  studied  the  diﬀerences  between  the  primary
and secondary infections of dengue in the presence of seasonality and multiple viral strains [1]. Kabir and
Tanimoto conducted a cost-eﬃciency analysis for the eﬀect of ADE on dengue vaccination [20]. In addition,
a number of other mathematical models for dengue are surveyed in a recent review article [2]. There is no
doubt that these modeling studies have substantially advanced our knowledge in the transmission dynamics
of dengue and in the design of eﬀective control strategies for this disease. However, the fundamental role of
the asymptomatic infection in dengue transmission within a heterogeneous host population is only partially
addressed  at  present.  Particularly,  our  understanding  of  the  intertwined  relationship  among  the  primary
and secondary infections, the asymptomatic and symptomatic states, and the diﬀerent age groups, remains
In  the  present  paper,  we  propose  a  new  mathematical  model  for  the  transmission  dynamics  of  dengue
based on the age-structured modeling technique. Age-structured models have been employed in many epi-
demiological studies and have provided useful guidelines for disease control [5,8–10,12,21,22,25,27,32,35,37,
38].  A  few  of  these  have  been  speciﬁcally  devoted  to  dengue  [12,22,27].  Our  proposed  study  diﬀers  from
the  prior  age-structured  models  in  the  integration  of  several  factors  that  are  important  toward  a  deeper
understanding of dengue dynamics. Our modeling framework will incorporate both mosquito-to-human and
human-to-mosquito transmission routes, will include both symptomatic and asymptomatic infectious hosts,
will place a special emphasis on the secondary infection from asymptomatic individuals, and will connect
all  these  components  in  an  age-structured  setting.  The  model  consists  of  a  strongly  nonlinear  system  of
coupled diﬀerential and integral equations, which will be rigorously analyzed throughout this study.

The  remainder  of  this  paper  is  organized  as  follows.  In  Section 2,  our  age-structured  dengue  model  is
described in detail. In Section 3, the basic reproduction number is derived and the stability of the disease-
free steady state distribution is analyzed. Section 4 is devoted to the analysis of the existence of the endemic
steady state distribution and the possible occurrence of a backward bifurcation. In Section 5, the uniform
persistence of the disease is investigated. Finally, conclusions are drawn in Section 6.

We have presented a novel age-structured model to investigate the transmission dynamics of dengue. Our
model  links  the  interaction  between  the  human  hosts  of  diﬀerent  ages  and  mosquitoes,  includes  both  the
symptomatic and asymptomatic classes, and incorporates the eﬀects of primary and secondary infections.
We have placed a special emphasis on the asymptomatic individuals and their interaction with mosquitoes
and other human hosts. Our results highlight the roles of the asymptomatic hosts and secondary infection
in shaping dengue transmission under a heterogeneous setting that couples the host and vector populations
and that involves diﬀerent age groups.
A detailed mathematical analysis has been conducted for this model using the basic reproduction number
R0 derived in Section 3. It is proved that the disease-free steady state is locally asymptotically stable if R0 <

1 and globally asymptotically stable if R0 < 1 − ς
for some ς > 0. It is also shown that when R0 > 1, there
exists at least one endemic steady state and the disease is both weakly and strongly uniformly persistent.
Numerical  simulation  results  conﬁrm  these  analytical  predictions.  Additionally,  suﬃcient  conditions  are
established for the existence of multiple endemic steady states when R0 < 1 which could lead to a backward
